thread.title: Netflix Stock Falls On December-Quarter Earnings Report

author: PATRICK SEITZ
title: Netflix Stock Falls On December-Quarter Earnings Report
text:
Internet television network Netflix ( NFLX ) late Thursday beat its forecast for new subscribers in the fourth quarter. However, Netflix stock fell in extended trading after the company's guidance disappointed.
X The subscription video-on-demand service added 8.8 million paying subscribers in the December quarter, bringing its worldwide total to 139.3 million. Netflix had forecast 7.6 million new paying subscribers.
The Los Gatos, Calif.-based company earned 30 cents a share on revenue of $4.19 billion during the period . Analysts expected Netflix earnings of 24 cents a share on sales of $4.21 billion. In the year-earlier quarter, Netflix earned 41 cents a share on sales of $3.29 billion.
For the current quarter, Netflix expects to add 8.9 million paying subscribers. It forecast earnings per share of 56 cents on sales of $4.49 billion. Analysts polled by Thomson Reuters expected Netflix earnings of 83 cents a share and $4.61 billion in revenue.
 Netflix stock fell 3% in after-hours trading on During the regular session, it rose 0.5% to 353.19. Netflix stock currently ranks No. 8 on the IBD 50 list of top-performing growth stocks.
Key content releases in the fourth quarter included new series "The Haunting of Hill House," "Chilling Adventures of Sabrina" and "The Kominsky Method." Netflix also debuted movies such as horror thriller "Bird Box" and Oscar contender "Roma."
Netflix Becoming Less Reliant On Reruns "As a result of our success with original content, we're becoming less focused on second-run programming." Netflix Chief Executive Reed Hastings said in a letter to investors.
Netflix sees its competition as broader than just streaming video providers.
"In the U.S., we earn about 10% of television screen time and less than that of mobile screen time," he said. "We earn consumer screen time, both mobile and television, away from a very broad set of competitors. We compete with (and lose to) 'Fortnite' more than HBO."
He added, "Our focus is not on Disney+, Amazon or others, but on how we can improve our experience for our members."
Netflix reported negative free cash flow of $3 billion in 2018 because of its heavy investment in original content. It expects 2019 free cash flow to be similar to 2018 "and then will improve each year thereafter."
Netflix Price Hikes Could Increase Churn On Tuesday, Netflix raised its monthly subscription fees for U.S. members by 13% to 18%, depending on the plan. Its standard plan, which offers two streams in high definition, jumped to $12.99 a month from $10.99.
Analysts said the move will raise average revenue per user, but also is likely to increase subscriber churn in the near term.
After years of heady growth in the U.S., Netflix may have entered "harvest" mode, Bernstein analyst Todd Juenger said in a report to clients earlier this week. But it's more likely that Netflix simply doesn't want to leave money on the table, he said. It is "collecting easily earned revenue from a service whose consumer perceived value far exceeds its price."
Netflix Stock Gets Price-Target Hike Earlier Thursday, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris reiterated his buy rating on Netflix and raised his price target to 400 from 370.
"Critical to Netflix's success is continuing to delight consumers with great content, an enjoyable experience and an attractive price," Morris said in his note to clients. "We are confident that the company can deliver against these goals, particularly as management remains focused on investing in technology, and employee and creative content talent."
Netflix currently competes with Amazon ( AMZN ) Prime Video, Hulu and AT&T 's ( T ) HBO, among others. New entrants into the subscription video-on-demand market this year are expected to include Walt Disney ( DIS ), Apple ( AAPL ) and Comcast 's ( CMCSA ) NBC.
However, retailer Walmart ( WMT ) has scrapped its plans to launch a new video streaming service, CNBC reported Thursday .
